query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high‐entropy alloys (HEAs), a uniform, multi‐element microstructure promotes the rapid formation and self‐regeneration of a continuous passive oxide film that both minimizes micro‐galvanic effects and reinforces the surface against mechanical damage, thereby governing resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy processed to yield a fine, homogeneous, nanocrystalline or dual-phase microstructure with evenly distributed oxide‐forming elements.
generation.intervention: Expose the HEA to controlled mechanical wear (e.g., via a pin‐on-disk or sliding wear test) while simultaneously subjecting it to a corrosive environment (such as an acidic solution or molten salt) at temperatures that allow passive film formation.
generation.conditions: Testing should be performed under conditions that promote passive film formation (moderate to elevated temperatures and chemical environments that are not so aggressive as to completely strip passivating layers) with identical stress, temperature, and corrosive exposure across samples.
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous, adherent passive oxide film that forms uniformly due to the alloy’s homogeneous composition, which minimizes the formation of micro-galvanic cells between phases.
generation.mechanism: The high configurational entropy in HEAs leads to a uniform elemental distribution that favors the formation of a self-healing oxide layer. This layer acts as a mechanical shield (reducing wear) and a chemical barrier (reducing corrosion) by limiting localized galvanic corrosion between heterogeneous phases.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under simultaneous wear and corrosion conditions, the homogeneously structured HEA will exhibit lower overall mass loss and shallower wear tracks compared to a baseline alloy with either induced microstructural heterogeneity or a lower concentration of oxide-forming elements. Both the independent contributions of wear and corrosion and their combined interaction will be reduced relative to the baseline.
generation.baseline: A comparison alloy of similar overall composition but processed to produce a less uniform microstructure (e.g., with phase segregation or micro-galvanic sites) or with lower levels of oxide-forming elements, thereby compromising continuous passivation.
generation.boundary: This prediction is expected to hold in environments that allow passive film formation and maintenance (such as moderate acidic or molten salt conditions) but may fail in extremely aggressive chemical environments or under mechanical stresses that mechanically disrupt the film beyond its self-healing capability.
generation.uncertainty: While the mechanism is supported by evidence of improved corrosion and wear behavior in homogeneous structures, the precise magnitude of reduction in degradation rates and the interplay of wear and corrosion components require further quantitative validation across different alloy systems and environmental conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples: one processed to ensure a homogeneous microstructure (and therefore optimal passive film formation) and a matched alloy where processing induces controlled microstructural heterogeneity (e.g., phase segregation leading to micro-galvanic coupling). Subject both sample sets to identical simultaneous wear (via a pin-on-disk apparatus) and corrosion (using a corrosive solution or molten salt environment) tests at temperatures that support passivation. Monitor the evolution of the surface film in situ via spectroscopy and microscopy.
measurements: Depth and morphology of wear tracks
Electrochemical corrosion current densities and potentials
Integrity and continuity of the passive oxide film (using surface analysis techniques such as XPS or SEM/EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the homogeneously processed HEAs do not show statistically significant improvements in both wear and corrosion resistance (i.e., similar or worse degradation rates, wear track dimensions, and corrosion metrics) relative to the heterogeneous baseline, or if in situ analysis reveals that no stable or self-regenerating passive film forms under the testing conditions.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract The corrosion behavior of the FCC Cr 18 Mn 27 Fe 27.5 Ni 27.5 high entropy alloy (HEA) after exposure to molten FLiBe salt at 700 °C for 1000 hours, has been investigated. Results show that the HEA lost a higher mass compared to the reference 316 H stainless steel due to the dissolution of Mn into the molten salt. The loss of Mn from the alloy appeared to discourage the dissolution of Cr in the molten fluoride salts which is widely recognized as the mechanism of corrosion degradation. Thermal exposure at 700 °C for 1000 hours also led to the precipitation of an additional BCC phase Cr 67 Fe 13 Mn 18.5 Ni 1.5 , which was confirmed by CALPHAD predictions. Subject terms: Structural materials, Metals and alloys

In this study, bulk samples of a CrMoNbWV high-entropy alloy (HEA) were obtained for the first time by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed (MA) powders at 1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C. Microstructure evolution, phase formation as well as wear and corrosion behavior were investigated. The MA powders’ phase composition was found to be represented by body-centered-cubic (BCC) solid solution. The solid solution partially decomposed to Laves phases under the sintering, such as Cr 2 Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb, and NbVO 4 -VO oxides mixture. The temperature increase to 1400 °C led to a grain coarsening of the BCC phase and decreased the Laves phase content accompanied by precipitation at the grain boundaries. The sintered samples showed high hardness and compressive strength (2700–2800 MPa) at room temperature. The wear tests demonstrated excellent results in comparison to conventional wear-resistant composites. The obtained samples also exhibited high corrosion resistance under electrochemical tests in H 2 SO 4 solution. The CrMoNbWV HEA has comparable mechanical and corrosive properties with the WNbMoTaV type HEA, but at the same time has a reduced density: CrMoNbWV—10.55 g/cm

Abstract Dual-phase high entropy alloys have recently attracted widespread attention as advanced structural materials due to their unique microstructure, excellent mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance. However, their molten salt corrosion behavior has not been reported, which is critical in evaluating their application merit in the areas of concentrating solar power and nuclear energy. Here, the molten salt corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was evaluated in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl 2 salt at 450 °C and 650 °C in comparison to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). The EHEA showed a significantly lower corrosion rate of ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205. Similarly, EHEA showed a lower corrosion rate of ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205. There was selective dissolution of the body-centered cubic phase in both the alloys, B2 in AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 and α-Ferrite in DS2205. This was attributed to micro-galvanic coupling between the two phases in each alloy that was measured in terms of Volta potential difference using a scanning kelvin probe.
